title: The Adventure Bike That Can Replace Almost Everything In Your Garage - Top Speed
content: If you’ve been blessed enough to have a garage full of motorcycles, then chances are that it looks something like this. A sport bike stands under a cover in the corner, ridden just twice since spring, because hitting the track requires an interstate journey, but touring isn’t its forte. A dirt bike lies behind it with flat tires and a battery tethered to a trickle charger. Parked out front is the tourer that has been doing the daily grind. Three bikes, barely enough time to maintain all of them, piling expenses, and only one of them that hits the road with some regularity. That’s a hard-to-admit reality of one person with multiple bikes. This article has been updated with more context on the bike's versatility and real-world performance. Trouble is, none of those three bikes could cover the other two. They are all specialized products for a given use case, and anything outside of that is a compromise that, at the very least, is annoying, and at best, is avoided. A genuine do-everything machine, then, has to clear a higher bar than any one of those three individually. It needs enough chassis composure and power delivery to feel legitimately quick on a road that rewards commitment. At the same time, it has to offer enough wind protection and ergonomic range to make hours between fuel stops feel routine rather than punishing. A middleweight ADV is a great solution to replace two or more bikes, but you might crave the power deficit it has against the sport bike. While there’s also the need for enough ground clearance and suspension travel to survive loose surfaces. Very few bikes meet these criteria. Fewer still do it without feeling like a compromise stacked on a compromise. BMW built the R 80 G/S in 1980 on the idea that one motorcycle could genuinely go anywhere, and the latest R 1300 GS pushes that idea further than any generation before it. The 1,300cc boxer-twin sits low in a two-part frame that uses the engine itself as a stressed member, a layout BMW has used since the platform's earliest days to keep weight centered. At $20,395, it costs more than a sport bike and a dirt bike combined in some cases, but it’s also the very point that it’s trying to make: that it might be the only bike a rider needs to buy for a long time to come. We’ll admit it: a full-size adventure bike doesn't exactly seem right for a one-bike garage, but that’s exactly what makes the BMW R 1300 GS special. And you don’t have to take our word for it, either. The bike has really proven itself out in the real world, showing it can do it all, including globe-trotting, off-roading, commuting, and even carving corners up a mountain road. Few bikes come close to proving everything the brochure says out in the real world quite like the GS. Let’s start with globe-trotting. Unless you’re living under a rock, you’d know that the GS is the benchmark when it comes to around-the-world bike rides. Yes, more reliable and sensible options exist, like the Kawasaki KLR650, but there’s a reason rivals still gravitate toward the GS. The bike has everything it takes to be a globe-trotter, including plenty of power, all-road capability, and reliability and easy maintenance. All of that comes down to how BMW has engineered the motorcycle, including its low center of gravity, unique telelever front suspension, maintenance-free shaft drive, and more. The R 1300 GS balances that personality with the genuine ability to have fun on the road. The best proof of this is that the R 1300 GS has set a hill climb record, which is usually reserved for much lighter sports bikes. Ridden by Greg Mansell, a slightly modified R 1300 GS broke a 15-year-old hill climb record at the Bouley Bay Hillclimb, clocking a time of 45.13 seconds, beating the previous record by 0.02 seconds. Heck, it outperformed the mental BMW M 1000 XR, demonstrating just how capable the GS platform can be. Adventure touring and canyon carving are two ends of a spectrum, but the R 1300 GS somehow does both exceptionally well. Yes, it is still not perfect. On trails, you will feel its heft, and on corners, it will be slower to turn in than a sports bike. But can a sports bike tour, or can most tourers set a hill climb record? Mostly not. That’s the reason why we’ve picked the R 1300 GS as the bike that can replace almost everything in your garage. Every R 1300 GS has four riding modes as standard in the form of Eco, Rain, Road, and Enduro, each recalibrating throttle response and traction control for a different kind of day in the saddle. The optional Dynamics package adds Shift Assistant Pro for clutchless gear changes, Dynamic Suspension Adjustment (DSA), a sportier brake setup, and a pair of Pro riding modes that push the same chassis toward opposite ends of what one motorcycle can be asked to do. One setting dials in for the canyon road. Another tackles the washed-out fire road. So true do-it-all capabilities in an ADV with optional extras that still cost less than some of its competitors. You could decide to throw everything at the big GS, and it’ll handle it with aplomb. Switch into Dynamic or Dynamic Pro, and the throttle mapping sharpens, delivering power right off the lightest twist of the wrist instead of easing into it the way Road mode does. Shift Assistant Pro, part of the same Dynamics package, lets the rider go up and down the gearbox without ever touching the clutch lever. So transitioning from the urban environment to a set of twisties is a fluid change from convenience to excitement. The optional DSA suspension firms up damping on the fly as lean angle and speed climb, holding the chassis flatter under hard braking into a bend than the standard setup. None of it turns a 523-pound adventure bike into a proper sport bike, but it closes the gap substantially. Enduro mode alone, standard on every R 1300 GS, already loosens the electronics' grip on loose surfaces, letting the rear step out a little without traction control slamming the door shut on it. Enduro Pro, unlocked through the same Dynamics package, goes further still. Tuned around aggressive knobby rubber, it dials back electronic intervention enough that a rider can power the bike through sand or loose rock on throttle input rather than on what the electronics allow. Riders chasing serious trail use can also swap the standard cast wheels for optional forged enduro wheels, shaving weight in the unsprung mass spinning at each end of the bike. It’s truly the most durable ADV for America. The R 1300 GS’ versatile range continues to hold up away from a canyon or a trail as well, and it’s exactly why it gets the respect that it does for catering to all kinds of riding duties. The standard seat sits at 33.4 inches, but optional low and high comfort seats swing that range from 31.5 to 35 inches, so the R 1300 GS fits a range of riders. Heated grips and a Tire Pressure Monitor come standard, and so does a sport windscreen that adjusts by hand for better wind protection at highway speed. Radar-based guidance backs the optional Active Cruise Control that holds a set following distance in traffic or on a long interstate stretch, cutting fatigue on both kinds of ride. Add the optional Vario luggage system and the same bike can carry a week of gear for the tour. None of this versatility matters if the engine underneath it can't rack up the miles to prove it. The liquid-cooled 1,300cc ShiftCam boxer-twin features double overhead cams and BMW's variable valve timing, filling out the power curve to 145 hp and 110 lb-ft through a six-speed gearbox and a shaft final drive. While previously infamous for reliability issues, BMW has come a long way to bust those myths. The shaft drive is the first reliability win on its own, since it skips the sprockets, chain lube, and midlife replacement a chain-driven system eventually requires. BMW also spaces oil change intervals at 6,000 miles and valve clearance checks at 12,000, a decently long interval to keep things refreshed after your continent-crossing antics are done. The boxer's cylinder heads sit out in open air on either side of the bike rather than buried under bodywork, so cooling and access both work in the engine's favor over a long ownership run. It’s also one of the reasons that the big GS actually costs less to own and maintain. None of that guarantees a trouble-free bike on its own, but it's a proven assimilation of parts and engineering that has carried generations of GS owners past six figures on the odometer, and there's no reason to expect this one to break that streak. The R 1300 GS’ closest rivals don’t seem to win outright. The Ducati Multistrada V4 undercuts it on price, is more powerful at 170 horsepower, but riding on 19-inch cast wheels hints at its road-to-light-trails focus rather than a complete all-round build. The KTM 1390 Super Adventure R swings the other way entirely, priced higher at $21,649 with a proper 21-inch spoked front wheel, and 9.45 inches of suspension travel at each end, tipping the scales more towards off-road terrain. While the 1390 Super Adventure S is nearly as road-focused as a road and track weapon. Neither rival is a huge compromise, as the inherent traits of an adventure-tourer remain intact and lots of versatility is built in by default. The Ducati is the sharper road bike; the KTM is an either-or situation, given the trims. But the GS is neither the fastest nor the most extreme of the three, but it's the only one that doesn't ever demand a rider to give up an entire category of riding. And that is the whole point of owning just the one. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. title: Is It Worth It? Karol G’s ‘Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour’ - Remezcla
content: Following the highly successful run of the Mañana Será Bonito Tour—which solidified Karol G’s global star power when it became the highest-grossing tour by a Latina and led to her becoming the first Latina to headline Coachella—the Colombian singer kicked off her “Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour” on Friday, July 24, with two sold-out shows at Soldier Field in Chicago, IL. The “Tropitour” isn’t just another stadium concert. It’s evidence that Karol G’s becoming one of the defining live performers of this generation while expanding what’s possible for Latines, but more specifically Latinas. Seeing La Bichota live and in command of a colossal-sized crowd makes it clear why she’s become a worldwide phenomenon: she combines spectacle, intimacy, and an unapologetically feminine vision in a way few artists currently can. The real impact of Karol G’s work isn’t the elaborate productions or sold-out stadiums. It’s how she has turned a genre that has historically sidelined women into a space where thousands of women see themselves centered. An hour before Karol G even took the stage, it seemed as if every single one of the 62,000 seats was filled and buzzing with fans (dressed mostly in orange and pink) eagerly waiting for her to take the stage. The Venezuelan artist Elena Rose opened the night with songs like “Caracas en el 2000,” “Gangsta Ángel,” and “Carteras Chinas.” The opening act on the “Tropitour” is set to change and will also include Becky G and Greeicy. A countdown clock appeared 80 minutes later on the massive screens, giving fans 3:15 minutes to get to their seats. The screams began long before Karol G appeared and only got louder as the show progressed. The concert opened with an animated video telling the story of a woman who remembers the power of her voice. The three-minute montage ended with the tagline “Forever wild, forever free,” before “Latina Foreva” was projected on the screen and the beat for the empowerment ballad dropped, signaling the start of an electric night. She then moved into a “Tropicoqueta” vibe for the song, complete with an elaborate headdress, massive feathers and climbing up an elephant-sized parrot to sing “Papasito.” The all-female group Mariachi Reyna de Los Ángeles came out playing Son de la Negra as the stage’s colors flashed to green, white and red for the Mexican flag, before backing Karol G up as she sang “Ese Hombre es Malo,” “200 COPAS” and “MAMIII” (sans Becky G). For the second half of her show, Karol G made her way down to the crowd and performed from a second stage located in the middle of the floor. There, she set off high-octane dance party vibes with Daddy Yankee’s “Rompe,” “Dile Luna,” Bandida Entrenada,” and “Ojos Ferrari.” From there, DJ Daiky Gamboa took over to remix some of Karol G’s hits that wouldn’t be performed live. It gave her time to get back to the main stage and do a costume change into the last set of her show. The pace began to slow down as she transitioned to salsa beats (her band played Willie Colón’s “La Murga” before jumping into Tusa) and began to wind down for the night. Fan interactions were sprinkled throughout the show, including one moment in which she agreed to send a lucky couple to Paris for their honeymoon. She ended the night with sweet, melancholy hits “Milagros,” “Si Antes Te Hubiera Conocido” and “Viajando Por El Mundo,” where fans held up their phones to make sure they made those final moments last. In terms of surprises, one of the highlights of the night featured a new song debut. Rather than take the stage for an encore, Karol finished the night backstage, projected onto the big screens, singing and dancing to her new song “Matadora.” This was my first time seeing Karol G in concert. I was a fan of her music but never considered going to see her live. However, during the Mañana Será Bonito Tour, my Instagram feed was constantly filled with photos and videos of friends at her shows having a blast. That was enough to pique my curiosity and get me to tune in to “Karol G: Tomorrow was Beautiful” on Netflix. Watching the documentary on the tour made me realize what she’s doing is rewriting the rules, and in the process, we get to watch history be made. She had to fight an uphill battle to get the Mañana Será Bonito Tour greenlit, and it ended up being one of the most successful endeavors for Latine music. Reggaeton is a male-dominated genre full of misogyny, obstacles, and hypersexualization of women. The space is designed to keep women out, and yet Karol has risen to the top. She’s done it with a smile on her face, owning her femininity, embracing and being unapologetic about her sexuality, with thousands of girly pop fans cheering her on along the way. While Shakira recently set the record for the highest-grossing Latin tour of all time with her Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour, Karol G is only the second Latina in recent decades to mount a global stadium tour of this scale. It’s a path laid out by Selena Quintanilla (which Karol pays homage to in the documentary and during night two of her Chicago stop) but still too few women at the top. The nearly two-and-a-half-hour show was an over-the-top spectacle with elaborate set pieces, vibrant colors, and heart-thumping beats that gave you no choice but to move your body. Critics took to social media to say the concert was a repeat of her Coachella performance, which I would have never known if I hadn’t read the comments. Even if true, it’s a show worth taking out on the road with its extravagant set pieces and the energy Karol, her dancers, and musicians brought to the night. Given she already mixed things up on night two at Chicago with visuals, fans can likely expect changes as the tour progresses. If these two sold-out stadium shows are any indicator of what’s to come, it stands to reason that Karol G’s Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour is set to break her own records and pave the way for a new generation of entertainers. title: BMW R 12 G/S GS Trophy Competition Bike Showcases Adventure Performance at Its Peak - stupidDOPE
content: Adventure motorcycles occupy a unique position within the broader motorcycle industry. Unlike purpose-built motocross machines or dedicated touring bikes, they are expected to perform competently across a remarkably wide range of conditions, from paved highways and gravel roads to technical trails and remote backcountry terrain. As the segment has matured, manufacturers have increasingly emphasized versatility, often marketing adventure motorcycles as machines capable of doing everything reasonably well. The challenge, however, lies in demonstrating those capabilities beyond carefully produced promotional campaigns. BMW Motorrad has long addressed that challenge through the International GS Trophy, its biennial off-road competition that places riders in demanding real-world environments where mechanical reliability, rider skill, and thoughtful engineering are tested under genuinely difficult conditions. For the 2026 edition, set against Romania’s mountains, forests, river crossings, and technical terrain, BMW has developed a dedicated R 12 G/S GS Trophy Competition Bike. Although this exact motorcycle will not be offered for public sale, its significance extends beyond exclusivity. Nearly every component used to prepare the competition machine is available through BMW’s own accessory catalog, effectively transforming the bike into a practical blueprint for enthusiasts seeking similar capability. That decision reflects a notable degree of confidence in BMW’s production platform. Rather than constructing an unobtainable factory prototype filled with bespoke racing parts, the company demonstrates what can be achieved using components that customers can realistically purchase. In doing so, the R 12 G/S GS Trophy Competition Bike becomes less a one-off competition special and more a compelling case study in modular adventure motorcycle design. The International GS Trophy has evolved into one of BMW Motorrad’s most influential proving grounds. Unlike traditional motorcycle racing, outright speed plays only a secondary role. Competitors navigate challenging terrain through navigation exercises, technical riding sections, endurance stages, and teamwork-oriented challenges designed to reward consistency and adaptability rather than outright horsepower. Those conditions provide meaningful engineering validation. Steep climbs, uneven surfaces, river crossings, loose rock, mud, and extended days in remote environments expose weaknesses that ordinary road testing may never reveal. The motorcycles must perform reliably under sustained physical demands while remaining manageable for riders with varying skill levels. By developing a competition motorcycle around production-based hardware, BMW effectively demonstrates confidence that its engineering philosophy extends beyond controlled demonstrations into authentic off-road environments. That credibility carries considerable weight within the adventure riding community. At the heart of the R 12 G/S sits BMW’s familiar 1,170cc air/oil-cooled boxer twin. Producing 109 horsepower and 85 lb-ft of torque, the engine reflects an increasingly uncommon philosophy in an era where many manufacturers pursue higher peak outputs through liquid cooling and more aggressive performance tuning. Instead, BMW emphasizes predictable power delivery. For adventure riding, this approach often proves more valuable than headline horsepower figures. Technical trails require smooth throttle response, controllable low-end torque, and mechanical durability rather than maximum acceleration. The horizontally opposed boxer configuration also contributes practical advantages. Its low center of gravity improves balance during slow-speed maneuvering while enhancing stability across uneven terrain. Although the engine’s cylinder heads remain visually exposed, decades of refinement have demonstrated the platform’s remarkable resilience under demanding conditions. The continued use of air/oil cooling also reinforces the motorcycle’s mechanical simplicity without sacrificing meaningful real-world capability. Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the GS Trophy Competition Bike lies not in what has been added, but where those additions originate. Nearly every modification comes directly from BMW Motorrad’s accessory catalog. Manufacturers frequently showcase concept motorcycles equipped with specialized racing components unavailable to ordinary consumers, creating an aspirational image that cannot realistically be replicated. The Competition Bike serves instead as an illustration of how thoughtfully selected factory accessories can transform an already capable platform into a significantly more specialized off-road machine. This accessibility enhances the motorcycle’s credibility. Owners interested in preparing their own R 12 G/S for extended adventure travel or technical trail riding can follow much of the same equipment strategy without relying upon custom fabrication or aftermarket experimentation. Adventure motorcycles inevitably balance two competing priorities. They must remain rugged enough for technical off-road riding while offering sufficient comfort for the extended highway journeys often required to reach those destinations. BMW’s Comfort Package addresses that dual-purpose expectation. Hill Start Control reduces stress during steep inclines, particularly when the motorcycle carries luggage or navigates loose terrain. Gear Shift Assist Pro enables clutchless shifting that improves riding efficiency while minimizing fatigue over longer distances. Heated grips extend riding seasons into colder environments, while cruise control significantly improves highway comfort during multi-day expeditions. None of these features individually redefine the riding experience. Collectively, however, they contribute meaningfully to rider endurance. Reducing physical and cognitive workload allows greater attention to navigation, terrain assessment, and overall safety throughout demanding journeys. The Enduro Package Pro shifts emphasis from comfort toward capability. Off-road tires provide the most immediately noticeable improvement, increasing traction across loose surfaces where conventional dual-sport rubber may struggle. The inclusion of an 18-inch rear wheel also aligns with established off-road preferences. Compared with larger road-oriented wheel configurations, this setup expands tire options while improving compliance over rough terrain. Handlebar risers further support standing riding posture, an essential technique during technical off-road riding that improves weight distribution, visibility, and motorcycle control. These modifications illustrate an important principle. BMW prioritizes ergonomic refinement rather than radical mechanical transformation. The motorcycle remains fundamentally recognizable while becoming substantially better suited to challenging environments. Adventure motorcycles frequently succeed or fail according to suspension performance. The R 12 G/S provides 8.2 inches of front suspension travel and 7.8 inches at the rear, complemented by 9.4 inches of ground clearance. Those figures position the motorcycle comfortably within serious adventure territory. More importantly, they reflect thoughtful compromise. Excessive suspension travel may improve extreme off-road capability while compromising stability, accessibility, and road manners. Conversely, insufficient travel limits rider confidence once terrain becomes increasingly technical. BMW appears to have selected specifications capable of supporting demanding trail conditions without sacrificing broader versatility. That balanced approach remains one of the defining characteristics of successful adventure motorcycle engineering. Visually, the GS Trophy Competition Bike draws heavily from BMW Motorrad’s long-standing adventure heritage. The Lightwhite paint, blue Motorsport tank striping, and distinctive red seat reference familiar BMW design language while avoiding unnecessary retro styling. Only the official GS Trophy graphics remain exclusive to competition motorcycles. Interestingly, that exclusivity serves more symbolic than functional purposes. Every mechanical improvement remains accessible to customers. Only the visual identifiers separating competitors from consumers remain unavailable. This subtle distinction reinforces the motorcycle’s authenticity. For enthusiasts, that represents a considerably more meaningful proposition than producing an artificially unattainable special edition. The BMW R 12 G/S GS Trophy Competition Bike demonstrates an increasingly thoughtful approach to product development within the adventure motorcycle segment. Rather than showcasing an unattainable factory prototype built around proprietary racing components, BMW uses the International GS Trophy as an opportunity to highlight what its production platform can achieve through carefully selected factory accessories. That strategy strengthens the motorcycle’s credibility by allowing riders to replicate much of the competition specification using components already available through the company’s catalog. The combination of the proven 1,170cc boxer twin, Comfort Package, Enduro Package Pro, generous suspension travel, and purpose-built ergonomics reflects a philosophy centered on balanced capability rather than exaggerated specifications. Every modification serves a practical objective, improving rider control, endurance, or confidence without fundamentally altering the motorcycle’s approachable character. Although the exact GS Trophy Competition Bike will remain exclusive to riders competing in Romania’s demanding 2026 International GS Trophy, its greatest contribution lies in demonstrating the versatility of the underlying R 12 G/S platform. By publishing nearly the entire build sheet, BMW invites adventure riders to view the motorcycle not simply as a competition machine, but as an attainable blueprint for serious exploration. It is a compelling reminder that genuine adventure capability often results from thoughtful refinement rather than dramatic reinvention. The BMW R 12 G/S GS Trophy Competition Bike is built exclusively for the 2026 International GS Trophy. Riders interested in the production R 12 G/S and its available factory accessories can learn more through BMW Motorrad’s official channels.

title: BMW’s Baby GS Might Be The Sweet Spot Adventure Bike - TRP | The Rakyat Post
content: We tried out BMW Motorrad’s next-generation baby GS and honestly, it would make a great beginner bike. Subscribe to our FREE Newsletter, or Telegram and WhatsApp channels for the latest stories and updates. For years, owning a BMW GS has been something many Malaysian riders aspired to. But while the iconic R 1300 GS is the dream machine for many, its premium price tag means it’s often a dream that stays parked in the showroom. That’s where the new BMW F 450 GS changes the conversation. Priced from RM39,900, the F 450 GS isn’t trying to replace its bigger sibling. Instead, it’s aimed at riders who have jobs to get to on Monday, errands to run during the week, and only have time for a quick escape on the weekends. It brings the GS badge to a much wider audience without demanding a luxury-bike budget. Let’s be honest. Most adventure bikes in Malaysia spend far more time on city streets and highways than they do crossing deserts or climbing mountain trails. Its 420cc parallel-twin engine produces a respectable 48hp, while the bike weighs just 178kg, making it considerably less intimidating than BMW’s larger adventure bikes. That lighter weight means it’s easier to manoeuvre through Kuala Lumpur traffic, squeeze into parking spots, or push around at the petrol station after filling up. It’s the sort of motorcycle you could comfortably ride to work every day before pointing it towards Genting Highlands, Fraser’s Hill, Janda Baik or Kuala Kubu Bharu once the weekend arrives. For those who enjoy the occasional camping trip or exploring backroads, it has enough adventure DNA to venture onto gravel roads without feeling out of place. One of the F 450 GS’ most interesting features is the optional Easy Ride Clutch. In simple terms, it lets you move off from a standstill without having to manually operate the clutch lever. Imagine that. You can ride a BMW GS like a kapcai. In bumper-to-bumper traffic, that means your left hand gets a well-deserved break, while slow-speed riding becomes less tiring and the chances of accidentally stalling the engine are reduced. The system still provides engine braking when you roll off the throttle, so it feels familiar to riders who are used to a conventional manual motorcycle. Combined with Shift Assistant Pro, riders can also change gears without using the clutch in many situations, making everyday riding smoother and more relaxed. BMW has packed the F 450 GS with enough technology to make it feel premium without making it overly complicated. It comes with a full-LED headlight inspired by the R 1300 GS, adjustable brake and clutch levers, riding modes for different conditions, traction control, ABS, a 6.5-inch TFT display with smartphone connectivity, and a USB-C charging port for keeping your phone topped up during long rides. Meanwhile, its long-travel suspension and upright riding position promise the comfort adventure bikes are known for, whether you’re spending an hour commuting across the Klang Valley or taking the scenic route to the east coast. The BMW F 450 GS isn’t about crossing continents — although it’s certainly capable of longer journeys. It’s about making the GS lifestyle more attainable. For the office worker who has always admired BMW’s adventure bikes, the young rider upgrading from a smaller-capacity motorcycle, or the weekend explorer who wants one bike that can handle city commutes and Sunday escapes, the F 450 GS feels like the most practical entry into the GS family yet. Not everyone needs 145hp or a motorcycle designed for riding around the world. Sometimes, all you need is a bike that’s just as happy filtering through Jalan Tun Razak on a Tuesday morning as it is chasing the sunrise in Bukit Tinggi on a Sunday. And that might just be exactly what the BMW F 450 GS was built for. Share your thoughts with us via TRP’s Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, or Threads. content: Do you have a comment or question? Send it to the Mailbag. Every Monday we'll post several comments and/or questions. Click here to submit a comment or question to Mailbag. Remember to include your name and town in the email. If Twitter / X is your jam, you can send a question to me that way as well. We are back — well, select Vikings players reported Sunday, and the remainder of the roster is due to report Tuesday — but it's pretty much time to roll out the ol' football. I appreciate folks accommodating me taking a break last week and made the most of the time during a camping trip "Up North" with my family and neighbors. A canoe trek and a separate kayak paddle while observing wildlife offered serenity, and we had plenty of laughs with the group. Fans will be able to hear from Head Coach Kevin O'Connell and new General Manager Nolan Teasley during a press conference scheduled for 12:30 p.m. (CT) Tuesday. Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores is scheduled for a presser on Wednesday, the first ramp-up day of acclimation practice; Offensive Coordinator Wes Phillips and Special Teams Coordinator Matt Daniels are scheduled to speak Thursday. Fans will be able to view the team on the field for the first time on Saturday when the team hosts Back Together Weekend: Saturday Edition. Visit vikings.com/camp for information. The organization is excited to host Legends Weekend as part of the opening festivities. View photos of the Vikings roster as of July 27, 2026. Since there's still a bit of time before we recap the O'Connell-Teasley presser and any on-field action, I wanted to include the links for our camp positional previews before getting to a few questions. How's everybody doing? Been a while since I wrote. I really liked the comments by Jason G. (on July 13). I agree that Brian Robison, E.J. Henderson, Carl Lee were underrated players, but Doug Martin at DE and Joey Browner at S were two of the best to play their positions! I also love to talk about the some of the underrated players that have passed through here. Henry Thomas at DT, Steve Jordan at TE, Sidney Rice at WR, Ed White at G and Korey Stringer at T. Welcome back to the conversation and good to hear from you. I sincerely appreciate everyone who helps keep the discussion of Vikings and NFL topics going during the lulls, and I always look forward to people who ramp up their communication as the season approaches and kicks off. My Vikings Entertainment Network colleagues look forward to relaying the sights, sounds and summaries of training camp as everyone readies for the 2026 season. Recognition for Martin's overall impact may have been reduced by some rough seasons for the Purple, but by the end of the '80s, he had helped the Vikings course correct. His 61.5 sacks ranked fourth in franchise history when Martin retired, trailing only Carl Eller, Jim Marshall and Alan Page, and the total still ranks ninth all-time. If not for Ronnie Lott and the run of Super Bowls by the 49ers, Browner would have been even more appreciated beyond Vikings fandom. Thomas and Jordan were key in helping Minnesota close the '80s and open the '90s with some strong seasons. Rice's 2009 season was one of the best a receiver could hope for, but his 83 catches for 1,312 yards and eight touchdowns accounted for roughly one-third of his career stats in seven total seasons. It does make one wonder what would have happened had he benefited from more continuity at QB. White stacked impressive performances for eight seasons with the Vikings and nine more with the Chargers, totaling four Pro Bowls. Stringer tragically passed away on Aug. 1, 2001, as he was following his first career Pro Bowl and preparing for his seventh NFL season. Colleague Lindsey Young will have a story on Stringer's legacy this Saturday on Vikings.com, and a recognition will be part of camp. Jim Lindsey. I remember him on the roster, and I used to have a card of him. I don't remember much from him as far as an offensive performer. I do recall him scoring a TD at the OLD outdoor stadium. The Lions partially blocked a field goal, and it rolled to the Detroit 1. A member of the Lions was blocking to keep the Vikings away from the ball hoping it would roll into the end zone for a touchback. The blocker's foot accidentally touched the ball, and it rolled into the end zone as a live ball. No one from either team noticed the nudge except Lindsey as he fell on the ball when it crossed the goal line. The other players looked uncertain at what happened until a ref signaled the touchdown. Was that the game Alan Page had a couple early flags on him that fired him up that helped lead to his MVP season? I recall Page scored three safeties that season with the third happening in a home playoff game against Dallas. I remember it was a home game against Detroit at Minnesota but not sure it was the same game. I also believe that stadium was the last one to have both teams on the same sideline. The team sent condolences this week to the family of Jim Lindsey, who passed away at age 81 on July 19 in his home state of Arkansas. Lindsey was drafted by the Vikings in the NFL and the Bills in the AFL in 1966, the year before the leagues began the common draft to prepare for the 1970 merger. He played a reserve role on offense and contributed significantly on special teams, serving as a five-time captain for the unit. His captaincy began in 1968 and ran through his retirement. The play remembered by Jason involved the kind of awareness and savvy that Hall of Fame Head Coach Bud Grant loved, and it's just one example of how Lindsey endeared himself to Grant. Here is a screenshot from the original play-by-play booklet from that game: Jason's memory also is correct in that Page had an interesting penalty sequence and responded with the dominance that resulted in him becoming the first defensive player to win NFL MVP and with one of three safeties that season (the other was against Buffalo). In going through the play-by-play from that game (included below), Page garnered a personal foul on a second-and-10. On the following snap, Greg Landry threw the ball out of bounds, but Page was penalized for roughing the passer, resulting in another first down. Page sacked Landry for a loss of 9 on the ensuing play to create a second-and-19. After a 5-yard offsides penalty against Carl Eller, Landry tripped for a loss of 11 (tackle credited to Gary Larsen) and Detroit suffered a 15-yard holding penalty added to the play to create a second-and-40 on which Page recorded a 4-yard tackle for loss. On third-and-44, Detroit dusted off a QB sneak (I'm laughing about this as I type it, and hopefully it adds to your reading enjoyment), which resulted in a gain of 2 before Page made the tackle. I went back and read the Star Tribune recap of the uncanny sequence involving Page. From Sid Hartman's Dec. 12, 1971, column, beginning with a quote from Grant: "It doesn't pay to get Alan Page upset. He has been having a super year, but when they called successive 15-yard penalties on him, he seemed to come up with a little extra, and he was a part of some big plays that helped us win the game." Page admitted that he got a little angry when the two penalties were called. "On the first penalty, I used the head slap on a Detroit lineman," he said. "This move is legal if you use it on the first step with an open hand. To my knowledge, I did that legally, but the official saw it [differently]. The second penalty was justified. It came on a pass play when Greg Landry threw the ball. I got my hands up high trying to block the pass. When I came down, I landed on the top of Landry's head." That season was the fourth in nine consecutive campaigns in which Page was selected to the Pro Bowl and his second of five First-Team All-Pro selections. The NFL MVP began being awarded in 1957, and the only other instance of a defensive player winning occurred in 1986 (Giants LB and Hall of Famer Lawrence Taylor). Page generously has allowed his MVP trophy to be displayed at the Minnesota Vikings Museum since the venue opened in 2018. I'm biased but believe it's worth a visit. View photos of the top 10 receivers of all-time for the Vikings. In your estimation, which players and maybe coaches are under a microscope of scrutiny during this Vikings Training Camp? Coaches and players are best served if they have a general confidence in their physical attributes, as well as the ability to block out external voices/forces beyond a player's control. That said, it's also at least somewhat helpful to understand players are not just competing with anyone else within the position group but also anyone else on the planet that a team could find to make it better. Thus, it's best to put the best foot forward and treat every day as a job interview. That can be true at any point in time but also the case when a new GM comes aboard. O'Connell has often expressed an interest in wanting to help each player reach the best version of himself on any day. That goes for him, as well. I think all coaches and players understand continuous evaluation and progress tracking, whether that's sure-fire starters and All-Pro players or those who are participating in their first pro camp. title: GS Retail Arranges Program for Rainbow Box Orchestra Members to Join Pyeongchang Daegwallyeong Music Festival - 스포츠조선
content:
By
																						
												SoHyung, Kim Members of the Rainbow Box Orchestra, sponsored by GS Retail, took part in the Pyeongchang Daegwallyeong Music Festival. The Pyeongchang Daegwallyeong Music Festival, a classical music event held in Pyeongchang, Gangwon State, is marking its 23rd edition this year. Under the theme of "Inheritance and Innovation," it opened on July 23 and runs through Aug. 2 across Pyeongchang, Gangwon State. The festival will feature a range of performances, including chamber music, solo recitals and orchestral concerts. It will also offer side events such as coffee and wine academies with artists. Rainbow Box, GS Retail's flagship cultural social contribution program, has been run since 2005 with Hope Friend Hunger Countermeasures. Now in its 21st year, the program has accumulated 5.45 billion won in donations and has supported instrument education and ensemble activities for more than 13,000 children at 755 local children's centers nationwide, helping them build emotional stability and develop artistic talent. GS Retail, which began sponsoring the Pyeongchang Daegwallyeong Music Festival in 2024, has expanded artistic experiences for Rainbow Box members through its collaboration with the Gangwon Art & Culture Foundation. This year, the company organized a two-day, one-night program for 26 participants, including Rainbow Box Orchestra members and instructors. They attended performances and a special lecture by mathematician Minhyong Kim, spending time experiencing classical music and a variety of arts and culture firsthand. Park Kyung-rang, head of the ESG team in GS Retail's policy support division, said, "We will continue our ESG activities so that Rainbow Box members can keep growing their dreams through diverse cultural experiences." title: How Many G's Do F1 Drivers Experience? 2026 F1 G-Force Data - Yahoo Sports
content: F1 drivers experience roughly 2 to 3G during normal 2026 racing laps, with braking events averaging 2.0 to 2.3G across the heaviest stops of the season. Spa produced the hardest braking zone measured so far, at 2.34G. The 2026 cars generate lower peaks than the 6G-plus figures quoted for the previous generation, because they run lighter and carry less downforce. Normal racing produces roughly 2 to 3G through most corners and straights. The hardest braking zone of the 2026 season sits at Spa, averaging 2.34G from 275 km/h to 93 km/h in 2.08 seconds. The softest braking zone among the nine circuits measured is Silverstone, at 1.78G. Standing-start acceleration averages 1.0G from 0-100 km/h and 1.4G from 100-200 km/h. The highest confirmed g-force in a modern F1 crash is 67G, from Romain Grosjean’s 2020 Bahrain accident. The 2026 cars run a minimum weight of 768kg, about 30kg lighter than the previous generation, with roughly 30 percent less downforce in cornering trim. Spa-Francorchamps produced the hardest braking of the 2026 season so far. The top five qualifiers there averaged 2.34G through the entire braking zone into the Bus Stop chicane, slowing from 275 km/h to 93 km/h in 2.08 seconds. Every figure in that graphic comes from F1 Chronicle’s analysis of official F1 timing data for the 2026 season: the median deceleration across the full braking zone for the top five qualifiers at each round, taken from dry sessions across rounds one to ten. That whole-zone average is a deliberate choice, and it explains why these numbers read lower than the peak figures quoted elsewhere. Instantaneous peak deceleration spikes higher for a fraction of a second at the sharpest point of a stop, but qualifying telemetry of this kind cannot responsibly be used to claim a specific peak. The averages here are lower because they measure something different, not because they are less accurate. G-force measures acceleration against the pull of gravity. One G equals the force a stationary body feels at rest on Earth; braking, cornering or accelerating at 2G means the body is being pushed with twice its own weight. A road car braking hard at a red light pulls about 1G. An F1 car under braking pulls more than double that. F1 generates such high g-force because of downforce. The front and rear wings, floor and diffuser press the car onto the track at speed, which lets the tyres generate far more grip than a road car’s. More grip means the car can brake later, corner faster and accelerate harder, and every one of those forces registers as g on the driver’s body and neck. Belgian Grand Prix standing-start telemetry from the top five finishers shows a 2026 car accelerating at 1.0G on average from 0-100 km/h, rising to 1.4G from 100-200 km/h. That climb is the counterintuitive part. A road car’s hardest acceleration comes off the line, when the engine’s torque advantage is greatest and there is nothing left to give as speed builds. An F1 car does the opposite. Downforce grows with speed, and grip grows with it, so a 2026 car accelerates harder at 150 km/h than it does leaving the grid, even though the engine produces roughly the same power throughout. F1 Chronicle’s breakdown of how much horsepower an F1 car has covers where that power comes from; this is what the car does with it once the tyres have grip to use. Spa sits at the top of the list at 2.34G, with Suzuka close behind at 2.22G and Shanghai at 2.18G. Miami (2.17G), Monaco (2.11G) and the Red Bull Ring (2.06G) fill the middle of the field, followed by Barcelona at 2.04G and Melbourne at 1.95G. Silverstone produced the gentlest of the nine measured stops, at 1.78G, for its biggest braking zone of the lap. Even Monaco, the slowest circuit on the calendar by average lap speed, produces a serious braking event: cars arrive at the chicane out of the tunnel at 282 km/h and shed most of that in a 2.11G stop. Canada does not appear on this list. That weekend fell outside the dry-session criteria this analysis uses, after rain affected track conditions. The 2026 cars are lighter and carry less downforce than the generation they replaced, and both changes show up directly in the g-force numbers. The minimum weight for 2026 is 768kg, about 30kg lighter than under the previous regulations. Cornering downforce, in the cars’ highest-downforce Z-mode setting, runs roughly 30 percent below the best 2025-specification cars. The 2026 regulations also introduced active aerodynamics, with drivers switching the wings between a low-drag setting on straights and a high-downforce setting through corners, so the load on the car, and on the driver, changes constantly through a single lap rather than sitting at one fixed level. None of this makes the figures quoted for 2022-2025 cars wrong. Those cars were heavier, ran more downforce, and produced the higher peak numbers still repeated across the web. They are describing a car that no longer exists on the grid. Race conditions push the numbers lower again. Drivers brake earlier and softer in the race than they do in qualifying, easing off sooner to harvest energy for the hybrid system rather than attacking the limit on every lap. F1 Chronicle’s Belgian Grand Prix telemetry analysis measured lift-and-coast beginning around 50 metres earlier in the race than in qualifying across the lap’s braking zones, one of the reasons the g-force a driver feels on Sunday sits below even the qualifying averages used in this analysis. Crash forces sit in a different category from racing g. They are a single violent spike rather than a sustained load, and the highest figures on record dwarf anything a driver feels in normal use of the car. Romain Grosjean’s fireball crash at the 2020 Bahrain Grand Prix remains the highest confirmed figure in modern F1. The FIA’s investigation into the accident found Grosjean experienced a peak of 67G when his car struck the barrier. Max Verstappen’s high-speed crash at the 2021 British Grand Prix, after contact with Lewis Hamilton on the opening lap, registered 51G. Further back, David Purley survived an estimated 179.8G in a 1977 crash at Silverstone, decelerating from 173 km/h to a complete stop in just 66 centimetres after his throttle stuck open, among the highest g-loads a person has ever survived in a recorded incident. Jules Bianchi’s fatal crash at the 2014 Japanese Grand Prix has no official g-force figure attached to it. The FIA’s ten-person accident panel found instead that his car struck a 6,500kg recovery vehicle at around 126 km/h, an impact so severe the panel concluded no realistic safety structure could have prevented what it called non-survivable decelerations. These numbers explain why F1 keeps investing in cockpit safety even as racing g stays flat or falls. A car only needs to protect a driver from 2 to 3G for 300 kilometres of racing. It has to protect them from more than 60G in the fraction of a second when everything goes wrong. Neck and core strength are non-negotiable for an F1 driver, because sustained cornering and braking repeatedly pulls the head and helmet sideways and forward for the length of a race. Drivers build that strength through rowing, cable work and isometric neck training, alongside the cardio base needed to keep those muscles firing deep into a two-hour race. Many teams also use G-force simulators and centrifuge-style rigs so drivers get used to the physical sensation of sustained lateral load before they ever feel it in the car. The HANS device, short for head and neck support, is the piece of safety equipment that makes the sport’s crash forces survivable at all. It secures the helmet to a collar worn around the driver’s shoulders, so that in an impact the head is restrained rather than snapping forward on the neck alone. Every driver on the 2026 grid wears one, a direct response to exactly the kind of forces measured in the Grosjean and Purley crashes above. Want more F1Chronicle.com coverage? It depends on the duration and direction of the force. David Purley survived an estimated 179.8G in a 1977 Silverstone crash lasting a fraction of a second. Grosjean’s 67G in 2020 and Verstappen’s 51G at Silverstone in 2021 both sit well below that figure but far above anything a driver feels in normal racing. title: Karol G’s Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour Is a Bold, Joyous Ode to Latina Power - Rolling Stone
content: There are many artists having what could easily be considered a “good run.” And then there’s Karol G, who kicked off her latest headlining stadium tour — Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour — with the first of two sold-out nights at Chicago’s Soldier Field on Friday. Loosen your hips, cue the fireworks, pyro, and ready the giant guacamaya. No for real, she sings atop one. The Colombian singer has continued to define new heights for herself since winning Best New Artist at the Latin Grammys in 2018. Nearly a decade into her career, she made history repeatedly: She’s become the first Latina artist to [insert incredible achievement in pop music here], from becoming the first female artist to reach number one on the Billboard 200 chart with a primarily Spanish-language album to headlining Coachella to holding 11 Guinness World Records for her record-breaking streaming numbers, tour sales and other milestones. She’s captained a handful of back-to-back international, headlining tours in the past five years – all preparing her for this, her largest, most intentional procession yet. The opening show at Soldier Field kicked off a trek that’ll take her to 63 stadiums across North and Latin America, as well as Europe through mid-2027. For just under two and a half hours, after an opening set from Elena Rose, Karol and her troupe of no less than 20 dancers delivered a proud, ambitious and emotional production on a massive stage reimagined as the Colombian mountainside and rainforest that magnified her historic Coachella outing. Her multilevel “cave club” came alive through four acts telling the story of a woman reborn and buoyed on a mission of self-discovery by her ancestors and the land. The scene at Soldier Field was awash in the colors of the sunset: bright oranges, exuberant pinks, glittering golds and huge floral prints. An intergenerational fanbase from all over the Latin American diaspora, folks arrived in their dancing shoes (for which, seemingly, no heel was too high for the occasion or walk across Museum Campus) and outfits that ranged from their country’s flags fashioned as skirts to recreations of the artist’s feathered sunglasses by Chrishabana. A celebration of, not only Karol’s influence but cultura that binds millions, she opened her set with “Latina Foreva” in a fierce declaration of the evening’s agenda, before rolling right along into favorites including “Un Gatito Me Llamo,” “Qlona” and “El Makinon.” It felt almost ironic that her tour would start the week when United States congressmen debated the meaning of “Latina power” in a House subcommittee meeting. If you needed a lesson, Karol came equipped. As Act II was introduced by a pre-recorded vignette featuring famed Mexican-American actor Edward James Olmos, both he and Karol spoke passionately about the commitment to family, friends, work, ritual and joy. Later, an all-female mariachi troupe joined for a handful of songs including the traditional “Negrita de Mis Pesares,” plus Karol’s hits “Ese Hombre Es Malo,” “Mamiii” (which she made into a global smash with Becky G),” and “200 Copas.” There were also indelible fan interactions, like a lucky couple who was promised tickets to another Karol concert in Paris for their honeymoon. One thing was clear: being a tropicoqueta runs deep. Sure, some transitions were a bit clunky. At one point attendees questioned if the electricity went out, but a few moments of silence quickly gave way to thumping congas, horns, and wood flutes from a live band that only seemed to grow as they played cumbias and porros. As dancers writhed and contorted themselves in an elongated sequence that took over a satellite stage disguised as a lagoon (ticketholders, you may be in the splash zone just FYI) and a DJ spun additional hits like “A Ella” and “Provenza,” Karol readied herself for the final act. Dressed head-to-toe in bejeweled orchids, she addressed and thanked her audience again. “Being Latino is the coolest thing in the world,” Karol said in Spanish to uproarious applause, before adding that life is really about the simple things. She flexed unexpected vocal acrobatics on “Si Antes Te Hubiera Conocido” and “Viajando Por El Mundo” to bring it all home. As dancers ran across the stage carrying kites and flags of all the countries in the Americas, confetti fell from cannons onto the crowd. At the end, she debuted her new single, “Matadora.” Confident, strong, sexy, secure, full of heart, Karol showed that being a “bichota” and “tropicoqueta” is a global movement. Find your own guacamaya and get on board. A broader private markets platform for high net worth clients aligns with the wider industry push to give wealthy investors more structured access to private equity, private credit and other less liquid assets. The AEGIS Hedging Solutions acquisition adds another piece to Goldman Sachs Alternatives, which is being developed as a diversified platform alongside the firm's existing public markets and advisory businesses. Together, these developments give investors more information about how NYSE:GS is working to deepen fee-based relationships and broaden its role across private markets and risk management services.
